aDifferentServerStartedServingThe: A different server started serving the segments.
aSegmentFromThePlaylistCould: A segment from the playlist could not be downloaded.
aViewerWouldSeeAStall: A viewer would see a stall for buffering: video arrives slower than it plays.
audioAbsentHow: At a look the decoder got the picture and found no sound track in the segment, and the stream has no playlist of sound to listen to next either. It is told after three such looks in a row.
audioAbsentWhat: The stream has no sound track: neither with the picture nor in a playlist of its own. This is told for information — the stream may never have had any sound.
audioChannelSilentHow: At every look the monitor decodes a couple of seconds of sound and measures every channel by itself. When one of the first two channels (left and right) is silent and the other plainly is not — no quieter than −50 dB — at three looks in a row, over a minute at least, the same channel each time, it is a finding. The other channels of multichannel sound are not counted: they are often silent with nothing wrong.
audioChannelSilentWhat: The sound of the stream has two channels and one of them is silent: the viewer hears the sound on the left alone, or on the right. It is usually a broken or wrongly patched connection on the way to the encoder.
audioFrameBytes: Size of a frame of sound, bytes
audioFrames: Frames of sound in the data
audioLevel: Sound level, dB below full scale
audioLoopHow: For the first frames of sound of every segment the monitor remembers a fingerprint of their coded bytes. A live encoder never codes sound into the same bytes twice; a recording going round does every time. When every frame of sound of five segments in a row, over half a minute at the least, was seen before, it is a recording going round. Silence does not count: it is coded the same every time. No decoding is needed for this.
audioLoopWhat: The sound of the stream goes round: the same frames of sound come again and again — a recording played in place of live sound. The picture does not go round with it (or there is none, as with radio).
audioQuietHow: At every look the monitor measures the level of a couple of seconds of sound. A quiet scene of a film can stay below −45 dB for twenty minutes on end, so this is concluded only when every look for two hours was below that level. Ordinary television keeps to about −27 dB.
audioQuietWhat: There is sound in the stream, far quieter than usual: the viewer has to turn the volume all the way up. It is not silence, which is told by itself.
audioSilentWhat: The playlists and the segments are in order, and the sound is silence.
audioUndecodableHow: Once in the set period the monitor hands the beginning of a segment to a decoder. When that data has half a second of sound or more by its container, a picture came out of it and no sound did, at three looks in a row, over a minute at least, the sound is taken not to decode. Sound that did not come out together with the picture is asked of the decoder by itself, so that an error in the video does not pass for one in the sound.
audioUndecodableWhat: The picture of the stream decodes and its sound does not: the container has frames of sound, and a decoder gets not a second of sound out of them. The viewer gets a picture with no sound, or a player error. Usually the encoder sends something other than what the sound track declares.
betweenTwoChecksSegmentsTheMonitor: Between two checks, segments the monitor never saw left the playlist.
bitsPerPixel: Bits a point in a frame between keyframes
distinctFrames: Distinct frames of sound in the recording
howPlaylistStale: The media sequence number of the first segment, the number of segments and the URI of the last one are compared. If they do not change for longer than the threshold (a multiple of EXT-X-TARGETDURATION), the playlist is considered stale.
howSequenceJump: The media sequence number of the first segment in the new playlist is compared with that of the last segment in the previous one. A gap means the playlist window moved further than its own length: either checks ran less often than the window lasts, or the origin dropped segments in one jump.
howSequenceRegression: The media sequence number of the last segment is lower than in the previous check.
inOfPlaybackTheOriginPublished: In {wall} of playback the origin published {media} of video: {pct} % of real time.
judgedBySizes: This is a sign, not an observation: nobody decoded the picture or the sound. It was judged by the size of the coded frames: a picture that does not change, and digital silence, code into next to nothing. Live television is never that small — of the samples of real streams the lightest was ten times the threshold. To know for certain, turn on the picture check with a decoder.
jumpAfterOutage: {since} passed between two successful checks; failed checks in between: {n} ({why}).
jumpBeyondWindow: The check came within that time, yet the segments were gone: the origin moved the playlist further than its own window allowed — dropped segments at once or rebuilt the playlist. Both playlists are in the snapshot.
jumpIsConsequence: The segments left the window while the playlist could not be read. This is a consequence of that failure, not a separate loss: the failure itself has an incident of its own.
jumpPromised: {since} passed between checks. By the playlist of the previous check a segment had to stay listed for at least {keeps} (its window less the longest segment).
lastSegmentInThePreviousCheck: Last segment in the previous check
lastStepTheBufferHeldAnd: Last step: the buffer held {before}, and {gained} of video arrived in {elapsed}, leaving it {short} short.
mediaUndecodableHow: Once in the period set, the monitor hands the beginning of a segment to a decoder. When three looks in a row, over a minute at least, got neither a picture nor sound, the stream is told to be undecodable. One look that failed means nothing.
mediaUndecodableWhat: The playlists are served, the segments download, the container is in order — and inside there is neither video nor sound: a decoder gets not one frame and not a second of sound out of the segments. A viewer sees an empty screen or a player error. Usually it is an encoder gone wrong, sending into the tracks something other than what they are declared to be, a stream left encrypted at the input, or garbage from the source.
noPicturesInTheVideoTrack: The video track carries packets ({rate} kbit/s) with next to no pictures among them: {pictures} in {packets} packets, where video has a picture in every packet. This is not video that failed to decode, it is not video at all. It does not look like encryption — the place to look is the encoder or the source of the channel.
noResponseToThePlaylistRequest: No response to the playlist request was received: a timeout, a dropped connection or endless redirects.
onAverageVideoArrivedAlmostOn: On average video arrived almost on time: the stall was caused by a one-off pause in the arrival of segments.
passedBetweenChecksASegmentIs: {since} passed between checks; a segment is guaranteed to stay in the playlist for {keeps} (the {window} window less the longest segment).
pictureBlackWhat: The playlists and the segments are in order, and the screen is black: the viewer gets a stream with nothing in it.
pictureDarkShare: Share of points all but black
pictureFrozenWhat: The playlists and the segments are in order, and the picture stands still: the same frame look after look.
pictureLookHow: Every few minutes the monitor decodes one keyframe of a segment and a couple of seconds of sound. One dark frame or a pause means nothing, so after a look that found something it looks again in 20 seconds; the conclusion is made when the same shows three looks in a row and for a minute at least. Between looks the picture is not seen.
pictureLoopHow: For every keyframe of a segment the monitor remembers a fingerprint of its coded bytes. A live encoder never codes two pictures into the same bytes; a clip going round does every time. When every keyframe of five segments in a row, over half a minute at least, was seen before, it is a clip. No decoding is needed for that.
pictureLoopWhat: The stream shows the same pictures over and over: a short clip started in place of the channel, usually a slate "for technical reasons…". The playlists and the segments are in order all the while.
pictureSlateHow: A slate is known in two ways. By the picture: every few minutes the monitor decodes one frame of the stream and compares it with the marked slates cell by cell; a match, no further off than the noise of coding, is the slate at once. By the clip: when a slate was marked in an incident "A clip going round", the fingerprints of the coded frames of the clip are remembered, and a stream that sends the same frames is known at the first segment, with no decoding.
pictureSlateWhat: A slate is on air in place of the channel: a picture somebody marked as an operator's slate. The playlists and the segments are in order all the while.
previousPlaylistKeeps: The previous playlist guaranteed a segment
renumberedHow: The number of the last segment in the previous playlist is compared with the numbers in the new one. A jump ahead counts as a change of numbering when the skipped numbers stand for three times the time between the checks plus a minute. Going back counts as one when the playlist came from another server.
renumberedWhat: The media sequence numbers in the playlist do not continue the previous ones: they went back, or jumped further ahead than could have been published in the time that passed. No segments were lost. It usually happens when servers behind a balancer number segments differently and another one answered, or when the packager was restarted and started counting over. A player that follows the numbers loses its place in the stream at that moment.
someOfTheNewSegmentsFailed: Some of the new segments failed to download, so they did not add to the buffer.
theCheckCameLaterThanA: The check came later than that although the playlist was read without errors in between: the monitor was late. This is a gap in observation, not a loss at the origin.
theCheckCameWithinTheWindow: The check came within the window, yet the segments were gone: the origin moved the playlist in one jump.
theFirstVideoFrameOfThe: The first video frame of the segment is checked for an IDR frame, a frame with a recovery point SEI or the random access indicator in the MPEG-TS header.
theHostThatReturnedTheResponse: The host that returned the response after all redirects is compared.
theHostThatServedTheLast: The host that served the last segment is compared.
theListOfVariantUrisIs: The list of variant URIs is compared with the previous check.
theListOfVariantsInThe: The list of variants in the multivariant playlist changed.
theMediaSequenceWentBackwardsThe: The media sequence went backwards: the origin restarted or is serving an old playlist.
theMonitorRemembersTheSegmentUris: The monitor remembers the segment URIs from the previous playlist and compares them by media sequence number.
theMonitorRunsAModelOf: The monitor runs a model of a player. It starts with a buffer of three EXT-X-TARGETDURATION; the buffer drains at real-time speed and grows by the duration of every new segment that appeared in the playlist and was downloaded successfully. When the buffer falls below zero, that is a stall. Once new segments appear, the model starts over.
theOriginChangedEXTXTARGETDURATION: The origin changed EXT-X-TARGETDURATION on the fly. The specification does not allow this, but players usually cope.
theOriginProducesVideoSlowerThan: The origin produces video slower than real time: stalls will recur for as long as it does.
thePlaylistOfALiveStream: The playlist of a live stream stopped changing: there are no new segments.
thePlaylistRequestWasAnsweredBy: The playlist request was answered by a different server than last time.
thePlaylistWasUnchangedForThe: The playlist was unchanged for {stale}; the limit is {limit}.
theRequestDidNotEndWith: The request did not end with a server response in the allotted time; the error text is below.
theRequestGoesToTheStream: The request goes to the stream URL and follows all redirects; the status code of the last server in the chain is what counts.
theSameMediaSequenceNumberNow: The same media sequence number now refers to a different file.
theSegmentDoesNotStartWith: The segment does not start with a frame that decoding can begin from: on switching to it a player will show artifacts or wait for the next one.
theSegmentDurationFromEXTINFIs: The segment duration from EXTINF is compared with EXT-X-TARGETDURATION, with a small tolerance.
theSegmentIsLongerThanThe: The segment is longer than the EXT-X-TARGETDURATION of the playlist allows.
theSegmentIsNoticeablyHeavierThan: The segment is noticeably heavier than BANDWIDTH in the multivariant playlist promises: a player that chose the variant by its declared bitrate may fail to download it in time.
theSegmentRequestDidNotEnd: The segment request did not end with a server response.
theSegmentSizeInBitsIs: The segment size in bits is divided by its duration from the playlist and compared with the BANDWIDTH of the variant. Segments shorter than one second are ignored.
theServerAnsweredThePlaylistRequest: The server answered the playlist request with an error status code.
theServerAnsweredTheSegmentRequest: The server answered the segment request with an error status code.
theStartOfTheVideoIn: The start of the video in a segment is compared with the end of the previous segment.
theStatusCodeOfTheResponse: The status code of the response to a request for a segment from the playlist is what counts.
theTimestampsAtASegmentBoundary: The timestamps at a segment boundary do not continue one another, and the playlist has no EXT-X-DISCONTINUITY tag.
theValueIsComparedWithThe: The value is compared with the previous check.
variantsApartHow: The end of the last segment of every video variant is compared by EXT-X-PROGRAM-DATE-TIME. Two target durations of difference are allowed: the playlists are read one after another, and one of them may already list the next segment. Media sequence numbers are not compared — variants may number their segments independently (RFC 8216, section 6.3.2). Without EXT-X-PROGRAM-DATE-TIME tags the check is not made.
variantsApartWhat: The video variants of one stream have drifted apart in time: one of them lags behind the others. A player switching to the lagging variant will not find the continuation there.
videoPackets: Packets in the video track of the segment
videoPictures: Pictures in the video track of the segment
